title: Brookhaven Lab and Stony Brook Demonstrate First US Free-Space Quantum Network Link Across 13 Miles - Quantum Computing Report
gist: Brookhaven National Laboratory and Stony Brook University demonstrated the first permanent free-space optical quantum link in the US, transmitting entangled photons 13 miles through open air using adaptive optics adapted from astronomical telescopes, and are now extending the network to Yale and toward satellite-based quantum key distribution, backed by a $300M state quantum hub.

insights.claim: Brookhaven National Laboratory and Stony Brook University demonstrated the first permanent free-space optical (FSO) quantum link in the United States, transmitting single photons and entangled photon pairs across 13 miles (21 km) of open atmosphere between Stony Brook's Quantum Watchtower and Brookhaven's Quantum Lighthouse.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Establishes a wireless complement to fiber-based quantum networks that other regional quantum networks may replicate as a template for extending reach without new fiber trenching.
insights.locator: Researchers at the U.S. Department of Energy's

insights.claim: The new free-space link adds a wireless leg to what is already the nation's longest metropolitan quantum network, a 161-mile, eight-node fiber-optic network spanning Long Island.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Signals the network is scaling as a hybrid fiber-plus-free-space architecture rather than fiber-only, widening the set of possible use cases such as mobile or satellite-linked nodes.

insights.claim: Turbulent ground-layer atmosphere — thermal variation, wind, and ground structures — distorts light wavefronts and causes loss of spatial coherence and single-photon coupling failures, which is the central engineering challenge for unguided free-space single-photon transmission.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: This is the core technical bottleneck any competing free-space quantum link effort must solve before free-space links can be trusted infrastructure.
insights.locator: Transmitting unguided single photons across low-altitude

insights.claim: The telescope and adaptive-optics system was developed by Brookhaven's Instrumentation Department by adapting astronomical telescope designs from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, expanding a 5-micron fiber core output to a 25-inch (0.6-meter) primary mirror beam and using kilohertz-frequency deformable mirrors to correct atmospheric turbulence in real time before refocusing light back into a 5-micron fiber core at the receiver.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Shows a reusable engineering pathway of cross-pollinating astronomical instrumentation into quantum networking hardware, lowering technical risk for future free-space quantum links.

insights.claim: On August 19, 2026 at 12:26 a.m. ET, Brookhaven's Quantum Lighthouse recorded the arrival of entangled photon pairs sent from Stony Brook's Quantum Watchtower across the free-space link, and the team subsequently demonstrated daytime precision transmission validating single-photon optical tracking and beam stabilization.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Daytime free-space quantum transmission is materially harder than nighttime due to background photon noise, so proving both makes the link operationally credible rather than a nighttime-only lab curiosity.

insights.claim: Unlike commercial optical fiber networks that require telecom-band wavelengths (~1550 nm), the free-space link can carry infrared wavelengths native to atomic systems and physical quantum processors, creating a direct channel to entangle remote atomic memories without wavelength-conversion overhead.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Removes a costly quantum frequency-conversion step that fiber-based networks require, a potential efficiency edge for free-space links connecting atomic-based quantum memories or processors.

insights.claim: A third identical optical facility has been built at Yale University in New Haven, Connecticut, and the team is preparing a 30-mile (48 km) free-space entanglement link across Long Island Sound to bridge New York and Connecticut quantum nodes.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Watch for the Yale link as the next milestone testing whether the technology scales to longer, over-water free-space distances.

insights.claim: The team, led by Stony Brook Quantum Institute Director Dr. Eden Figueroa and Brookhaven scientist Justine Haupt, plans to use the same rooftop telescope infrastructure to track classical and quantum low-Earth-orbit satellites, laying ground-station groundwork for satellite-based quantum key distribution (QKD) and distributed quantum computing.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Positions this ground infrastructure as a reusable asset for future satellite quantum networks, a longer-horizon bet on space-based QKD that could extend the network's reach beyond fixed regional nodes.

insights.claim: The project is supported by the DOE Office of Science, the National Science Foundation, and New York's Empire State Development, which funded the $300 million SUNY Stony Brook Quantum Innovation Hub.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
entities: SUNY Stony Brook Quantum Innovation Hub
insights.so_what: Signals substantial state and federal capital committed to this specific regional quantum network, indicating a well-funded strategic program rather than a small university experiment.
insights.locator: Supported by the DOE Office of Science

insights.claim: The milestone is framed as advancing regional distributed quantum networks under the U.S. Department of Energy's Genesis Mission framework.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Ties a specific lab demonstration to a named federal strategic initiative, useful for tracking how DOE Genesis Mission funding translates into concrete quantum infrastructure.
